correctness.rationale: A nonzero zero-divisor has nonempty proper support. Products vanish exactly for disjoint supports, so support cells are independent and duplicating a selected vertex within its cell creates no edge. A maximum independent set therefore takes whole cells, and the admissible support families are pairwise intersecting. Each complement pair gives a separate upper bound by the larger cell weight. Independently of logarithms, put P=∏a_i. A heavier or tied cell has weight at least √P. If two such supports are disjoint, their weight product equals the weight of their union and is at most P; because every a_i>1, equality requires a full union and two ties. Thus the only conflicts among heavier or tied supports are the tied complementary pairs themselves. Selecting exactly the stated sides achieves the bound, with all choices at ties independent; positivity forces every equality case to have this form. Summing the two weights of each pair counts N, and passing from unordered to ordered supports yields the factor 1/4. At (3,4,7) the two strict-heavy cells contribute 12 and 18 and the one tied pair contributes 6, giving 36 and two maximizers.
residual_risks: The replay enumerates only full choices from complement pairs and is not a proof that an optimum must make full choices; the upper-bound and attainment argument gives that implication. The independent-tie classification is not asserted when some a_i=1.

Frankl and Tokushige section 10, Example 10.3 and Theorem 10.4 give the product-measure formulation and cross-intersecting results in different parameter ranges.

value.rationale: Maximum independent sets in direct products of fields are natural ring-graph objects. The result gives an exact arbitrary-rank rule for both optimal size and nonuniqueness, and explains how multiplicative balance of field-unit counts governs nonuniqueness without separate rank-by-rank casework. Knowing exactly which cells persist or can switch is useful beyond the scalar independence number.
residual_risks: The stated contribution excludes binary factors and does not settle more general product measures or other associated ring graphs.
